subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In sociology, 'norms' are best defined as:
options: Broad beliefs about what is important and worthwhile
Specific rules or expectations guiding behaviour in particular situations
questions.explain: Norms are specific guidelines for behaviour in given situations, whereas values are broader beliefs.

questions.q: 'Resocialisation' refers to:
options: Learning norms and values for the very first time as a baby
Learning new norms and values, often after entering a new environment like prison or the army
questions.explain: Resocialisation is learning new and different norms and values, often when entering an institution such as the army or prison.

questions.q: 'Cultural diversity' within a society means:
options: The existence of different cultures, beliefs and lifestyles within one society
Everyone shares exactly the same culture
questions.explain: Cultural diversity refers to the variety of cultures, beliefs and ways of life existing within a single society.

questions.q: 'Beliefs' as part of culture are best described as:
options: Ideas that people hold to be true about the world
questions.explain: Beliefs are the ideas and convictions people hold to be true, forming part of a society's culture.

questions.q: How is national identity typically reinforced?
options: Through symbols such as flags, anthems, language and shared history
Only through a person's blood type
questions.explain: National identity is socially constructed and reinforced through symbols such as flags, anthems, language, traditions and shared history.

questions.q: The study of 'feral children' is often used to support the idea that:
options: Children need no contact with others
Much human behaviour is learned through socialisation (nurture)
questions.explain: Feral children, raised without normal human contact, suggest that much human behaviour must be learned through socialisation.

questions.q: A 'high culture' is often contrasted with popular culture because high culture is seen as:
options: Enjoyed by the mass of ordinary people
Associated with elite tastes such as opera and classical art
questions.explain: High culture refers to products and tastes (e.g. opera, classical art) associated with social elites, contrasted with popular culture.

questions.q: A 'subculture' is:
options: A culture from another country only
A smaller group within society that shares some distinctive norms and values
questions.explain: A subculture is a group within the wider society whose norms and values differ in some ways from the mainstream.

questions.q: The social construction of gender identity suggests that:
options: Gender has no link to society
Only adults have a gender identity
Masculinity and femininity are largely learned through socialisation, not just biology
Gender is fixed entirely by genes
questions.explain: Sociologists argue gender identity is socially constructed, with masculine and feminine roles learned through socialisation.

questions.q: The 'nature versus nurture' debate is about whether behaviour is shaped more by:
options: Biology/genetics versus social environment and learning
questions.explain: The nature-nurture debate concerns the relative influence of inherited biology versus social environment on behaviour.

questions.q: In sociology, 'culture' refers to:
options: Only art galleries and classical music
The whole way of life of a group, including its norms, values, beliefs and customs
questions.explain: Culture is the entire way of life shared by a group, including its norms, values, customs and beliefs.

questions.q: The workplace, with its norms and expectations, acts as:
options: A primary agent of socialisation in infancy
An agent that has no influence on adults
questions.explain: The workplace is an agent of secondary socialisation, teaching adults the norms and values expected in their job.

questions.q: A 'social role' is best described as:
options: The expected pattern of behaviour attached to a particular status (e.g. teacher, parent)
questions.explain: A social role is the set of behaviours expected of someone occupying a particular social position or status.

questions.q: 'Primary socialisation' takes place mainly through:
questions.explain: Primary socialisation happens in early childhood, mainly within the family.

questions.q: The way age identity is socially constructed is shown by the fact that:
options: Only children have an age identity
Age is purely a number with no social meaning
Age has the same meaning everywhere always
Expectations of 'youth' or 'old age' vary between societies and over time
questions.explain: Age identity is socially constructed because the meanings and expectations attached to ages differ across cultures and historical periods.

questions.q: 'Identity' in sociology refers to:
options: How individuals see themselves and are seen by others, shaped by factors like gender and ethnicity
A person's exact height and weight
questions.explain: Identity is the sense of who we are, formed through social factors such as gender, ethnicity, class and culture.

questions.q: Which is an example of how the media can act as an agent of socialisation?
options: Presenting role models and ideas that shape values and behaviour
questions.explain: The media socialises by presenting role models, norms and values that can influence audiences' attitudes and behaviour.

questions.q: 'Class identity' may be expressed through:
options: A person's accent, leisure activities and consumption patterns
questions.explain: Class identity can be displayed through markers such as accent, tastes, leisure pursuits and patterns of consumption.

questions.q: Religion can act as an agent of socialisation by:
options: Replacing the family entirely from birth
Teaching moral codes, beliefs and values to its followers
questions.explain: Religion socialises members by transmitting moral codes, beliefs and values that guide behaviour.

questions.q: 'Values' differ from norms because values are:
options: General beliefs about what is good, important or worthwhile
questions.explain: Values are general, widely held beliefs about what is desirable, while norms are the specific rules that put values into practice.

questions.q: A 'counter-culture' is a subculture that:
options: Actively opposes or rejects the dominant values of mainstream society
questions.explain: A counter-culture is a subculture whose norms and values strongly oppose those of the wider mainstream society.

questions.q: 'Secondary socialisation' is carried out by agents such as:
questions.explain: Secondary socialisation occurs later through agents beyond the family, such as school, peer groups, media and religion.
